extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / educated public interested in manners, moral essays, and literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short periodical moral and conduct essays in the Spectator tradition: concise, witty pieces that judge character, taste, and social practices while instructing readers about virtue and good sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value talents by their application to virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gifts of Nature and Accomplishments of Art are valuable, but as they are exerted in the Interest of Virtue, or governed by the Rules of Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not admire talent in the abstract; judge persons by how they apply their gifts. Praise ought to follow use: a painter or sculptor should be esteemed for the purpose as well as the execution of his designs. The passage urges writers and critics to weigh moral aim and social utility when appraising excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be carried away by mere beauty or wit
rubrics_metrics.description: When we suffer our selves to be thus carried away by meer Beauty, or meer Wit... there cannot be a more abject Slavery in this World, than to doat upon what we think we ought to contemn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before granting admiration, take notice of a person's disposition. External charms (beauty, wit) can mislead; the essay recommends abstracting the mind from mere appearance and not approving anything that does not promote goodness and honour. Practical examples: coquetry, vain dress, or ostentatious discourse should diminish our esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention should be the measure of approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the Intention stedfastly considered, as the Measure of Approbation, all Falsehood would soon be out of Countenance; and an Address in imposing upon Mankind, would be as contemptible in one State of Life as another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by motive: skill used to deceive or to serve unjust ends should not be praised. The essay contrasts eloquence used to defend an unjust cause with resolution in an assassin to stress that praise must follow intention and moral alignment, not mere effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve virtue against calumny; accept criticism with patience
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one thing necessary to keep the Possession of true Glory, which is, to hear the Opposers of it with Patience, and preserve the Virtue by which it was acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True greatness is steadiness of conscience and self-approval rather than dependence on public applause. Maintain the virtue that produced your reputation, endure detractors patiently, and do not pursue fame for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts should be judged for purpose as well as execution
rubrics_metrics.description: How many lewd Devices have been preserved from one Age to another, which had perished as soon as they were made, if Painters and Sculptors had been esteemed as much for the Purpose as the Execution of their Designs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating artistic work, consider whether it promotes modesty, truth, and humane sentiments. The author warns that valuing execution without regard to moral purpose preserves indecent or harmful images (satyrs, monsters), and counsels critics and patrons to prefer art with noble ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid encouraging amusements that degrade human dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or no they are not guilty, in some measure, of an Affront to their Species, in treating after this manner the Human Face Divine, and turning that Part of us, which has so great an Image impressed upon it, into the Image of a Monkey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not endorse public prizes or entertainments (e.g., 'grinning matches', races of asses) that make a mockery of human dignity or inspire senseless ambitions among the populace. Consider the moral as well as the entertainment value before patronizing or publicizing such diversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numbers to measure prudence and success
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers are so much the Measure of every thing that is valuable, that it is not possible to demonstrate the Success of any Action, or the Prudence of any Undertaking, without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ventures (commerce, hunting, hospitality), quantify costs and returns; merchants' skill with numbers is legitimate and socially valuable. Authors and moralists here advise practical calculation—returns, expenses, freight, customs, profit—rather than vain notions of honour unsupported by numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge economic actors by contribution and honest method
rubrics_metrics.description: He takes nothing from the industrious Labourer; he pays the poor Man for his Work; he communicates his Profit with Mankind; by the Preparation of his Cargo and the Manufacture of his Returns, he furnishes Employment and Subsistence to greater Numbers than the richest Nobleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate merchants and traders not by class prejudice but by the social benefits of their honest industry: employment, markets, and legitimate profit. The passage counsels against scorn for commerce when it serves public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify fashions and resist provincial impostures
rubrics_metrics.description: What I would humbly propose to the Publick is, that there may be a Society erected in London, to consist of the most skilful Persons of both Sexes, for the Inspection of Modes and Fashions; and that hereafter no Person or Persons shall presume to appear singularly habited in any Part of the Country, without a Testimonial... that their Dress is answerable to the Mode at London.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of purported 'London fashions' in the country; value authenticity and authoritative inspection to avoid being duped by false modes. While satirical, the advice highlights a criterion of verifying sources before endorsing trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prudent in raillery—know your company and your wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Rule I can lay down for them to avoid the like Calamities for the future, is thoroughly to consider not only Whether their Companions are weak, but Whether themselves are Wits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before engaging in playful mockery or repartee ('playing a Butt'), assess whether your companions can be safely teased and whether you truly possess the wit to sustain the exchange. Social humor requires self-knowledge and situational awareness to avoid humiliation.
